article_title: How Your Phone Knows Your Location Even With GPS Off
claim: GPS satellites orbit roughly 20,000 km overhead and a phone needs signals from at least four of them to triangulate a position.
source: GPS.gov (National Coordination Office for Space-Based PNT), Space Segment
required_correction: None. Actual altitude is ~20,200 km (MEO); "roughly 20,000 km" is a fair approximation. The 24-satellite constellation is designed so at least 4 are visible from any point, matching the article's minimum-four claim.

article_title: How Your Phone Knows Your Location Even With GPS Off
claim: GPS is slow to lock on, sometimes taking 30 seconds or more from a cold start.
source: Wikipedia "Time to first fix"; u-blox support forum
required_correction: Directionally correct but understated as a ceiling. Cold-start time-to-first-fix is commonly cited around 30 seconds under good conditions but can commonly run into the 2-4 minute range in practice; consider softening "30 seconds or more" to reflect it can be considerably longer, not just marginally so.

article_title: How Your Phone Knows Your Location Even With GPS Off
claim: WiFi positioning is often accurate to within 20-50 meters indoors.
source: Mapsted / Navigine / BlueFletch indoor positioning industry explainers
required_correction: The 20-50m figure is a commonly cited range for basic AP-proximity-based WiFi positioning (the kind Google/Apple's crowdsourced MAC-address databases use), but it's on the pessimistic side of what's achievable today — WiFi fingerprinting can reach 5-15m and WiFi RTT/FTM (802.11mc) can reach 1-2m on supporting devices. Not wrong, but could note modern best-case accuracy is tighter.

article_title: How Your Phone Knows Your Location Even With GPS Off
claim: Cell tower triangulation is usually accurate to a few hundred meters to a couple of kilometers depending on tower density.
source: RF Wireless World, Cellular Tower Triangulation explainer
required_correction: None. Industry consensus cites roughly 50-300m in dense urban areas and up to several kilometers in rural/low-tower-density areas, consistent with the article's stated range.

article_title: How Your Phone Knows Your Location Even With GPS Off
claim: Bluetooth beacons can pinpoint location to within 1-5 meters where deployed.
source: NCBI/PMC, "A Practice of BLE RSSI Measurement for Indoor Positioning"
required_correction: None. Commercial BLE beacon studies generally report sub-5-meter accuracy under normal deployment conditions, consistent with the article's figure.

article_title: How Your Phone Knows Your Location Even With GPS Off
claim: Emergency location for calling 112 is designed to bypass user location toggles entirely, because regulators require emergency services to be able to locate a phone that dials for help.
source: Department of Telecommunications, Panic Button and GPS Facility in Mobile Phone Handsets (Amendment) Rules, 2017; Android Emergency Location Service / Apple Emergency SOS documentation
required_correction: None. India's DoT rules mandated GPS in all mobile handsets from Jan 2018 tied to panic-button/emergency location, and both Android's Emergency Location Service and Apple's Emergency SOS are documented to override the device location toggle specifically for emergency calls/texts — matching the article's claim precisely. This is the article's flagged benchmark detail and it holds up.

article_title: How Your Phone Knows Your Location Even With GPS Off
claim: Android and iOS distinguish "precise" (GPS-level) from "approximate" (WiFi/cell-tower level, typically accurate to a few hundred meters to a couple of kilometers) location permissions.
source: Android Developers, Request location permissions; How-To Geek explainer on Android 12 precise/approximate location
required_correction: The precise/approximate distinction itself is accurate (Android 12+ and iOS 14+ both implement it), but the stated accuracy floor is a bit generous. Android's official approximate location has a documented minimum accuracy radius of about 2 km, and iOS reduced-accuracy locations are documented as 1-20 km — both coarser at the low end than "a few hundred meters" implies.

article_title: How Your Phone Knows Your Location Even With GPS Off
claim: Airplane mode cuts cellular, WiFi, and Bluetooth radios simultaneously.
source: Apple Support, "Use Airplane Mode on your iPhone"
required_correction: None, though worth noting both iOS and Android let a user manually re-enable WiFi and/or Bluetooth individually while airplane mode is on — which the article already accounts for by separately recommending the WiFi/Bluetooth scanning sub-toggle.

article_title: How Autocorrect Actually Decides What You Meant to Type
claim: Keyboards track the exact x/y coordinate of a touch relative to the center of each key (a spatial probability model), rather than just registering which key was pressed.
source: USPTO patent documentation on iOS/QuickType spatial-model touch keyboards
required_correction: None. Documented spatial models (e.g., bivariate Gaussian per key) compute key-selection probability from touch-point distance to key centers, matching the article's description.

article_title: How Autocorrect Actually Decides What You Meant to Type
claim: A language model scores how likely a word is given the words before it, which is why the same typed word can be corrected differently depending on sentence context.
source: Google Research, "The Machine Intelligence Behind Gboard"
required_correction: None. Context-conditioned language modeling for correction/prediction is exactly how Gboard's decoder is documented to work.

article_title: How Autocorrect Actually Decides What You Meant to Type
claim: Both iOS and Android keyboards maintain a personal dictionary of words a user types repeatedly, including names and slang, that eventually stop being "corrected."
source: Android Police, Gboard personal dictionary guide; SwiftKey learning-behavior documentation
required_correction: None. Gboard, SwiftKey and iOS keyboards are all documented to build a personal/dynamic vocabulary from repeated typed words that stops being flagged or auto-corrected.

article_title: How Autocorrect Actually Decides What You Meant to Type
claim: Newer keyboard engines (Gboard, SwiftKey, Apple's) increasingly use on-device neural network models rather than older statistical n-gram models.
source: Google Research, "The Machine Intelligence Behind Gboard"; arXiv, "Neural Search Space in Gboard Decoder"
required_correction: None. Google documents Gboard's evolution from n-gram statistical models to on-device neural language models (including transformer-based grammar correction on Pixel devices).

article_title: How Autocorrect Actually Decides What You Meant to Type
claim: Password fields are usually excluded from autocorrect by design, but username or email fields sometimes aren't.
source: Apple Developer Forums discussion of secureTextEntry/UITextInputTraits behavior
required_correction: Directionally correct and consistent with standard iOS/Android platform behavior (secure text fields disable autocorrection by default), but this claim would benefit from citing Apple's/Google's own developer documentation directly rather than a forum thread, which is the strongest source found in this pass.

article_title: How Autocorrect Actually Decides What You Meant to Type
claim: Code-switching between languages (mixing Hindi/regional words with English, very common in Indian typing) confuses the language model because it's scoring against patterns from formal, common text.
required_correction: Plausible and consistent with general knowledge that language models trained predominantly on monolingual/formal corpora perform worse on code-switched or informal text, but no Gboard/SwiftKey-specific benchmark or India-specific study was found to confirm this precisely. Consider softening from a flat assertion to "widely reported" or similar, or sourcing a specific study if one exists.

article_title: How Autocorrect Actually Decides What You Meant to Type
claim: Gesture/swipe typing decodes a continuous, noisy swipe path into a likely letter sequence before any word-level scoring even begins, adding an extra layer of ambiguity.
source: Grammarly Engineering Blog, "How We Use Deep Learning for Swipe Typing on the Grammarly iOS Keyboard"
required_correction: None. Swipe/gesture decoding is documented as a distinct shape-recognition step feeding into subsequent word-level language modeling, matching the article's description.

article_title: How Streaming Quality Adjusts Automatically to Your Internet Speed
claim: Video is encoded into multiple quality tiers broken into small chunks (roughly two to ten seconds), with HLS (used heavily by Apple platforms) and MPEG-DASH being the two dominant adaptive bitrate streaming standards.
source: Bitmovin, "Optimal Adaptive Streaming Formats: MPEG-DASH & HLS Segment Length"
required_correction: None. HLS's default segment length is 6 seconds and MPEG-DASH segments commonly run 2-10 seconds (optimal 2-4s), both falling within the article's stated "two to ten second" range. HLS-as-Apple-standard and DASH-as-the-other-major-standard framing is accurate.

article_title: How Streaming Quality Adjusts Automatically to Your Internet Speed
claim: Netflix and YouTube each use proprietary adaptive bitrate algorithms that balance picture quality against the risk of a buffer running dry and causing a stall.
source: Academic literature on buffer-based ABR (BOLA), which Netflix's approach is derived from/tested against
required_correction: None. Netflix has publicly discussed using proprietary buffer-based ABR logic influenced by/tested alongside academic approaches like BOLA, balancing quality maximization against rebuffer avoidance, matching the article's description.

article_title: How Streaming Quality Adjusts Automatically to Your Internet Speed
claim: Locking quality manually is available on YouTube, and on Netflix through account-level data-usage settings (Low/Medium/High/Auto), applied across the account rather than per device.
source: Netflix Help Center, "How to control how much data Netflix uses"
required_correction: None. Netflix's playback/data-usage setting is confirmed to be account (and per-profile) level rather than per-device, exactly as the article states.

article_title: How Streaming Quality Adjusts Automatically to Your Internet Speed
claim: Live streaming platforms typically run a much smaller buffer than on-demand video to minimize the delay behind the actual live moment.
source: Cloudinary, "Low-Latency Video Streaming Explained"
required_correction: None. On-demand/standard streaming often buffers 8-30+ seconds ahead for reliability, while low-latency live protocols (LL-HLS, WebRTC) target 2-5 seconds or less, confirming the buffer-size/latency tradeoff the article describes.

article_title: How Streaming Quality Adjusts Automatically to Your Internet Speed
claim: Downloading content ahead of time for offline viewing (available on Netflix, YouTube Premium, and others) removes the adaptive streaming/buffer-watching problem entirely since the full file is already stored locally.
source: Netflix Help Center (offline downloads); YouTube Premium product documentation
required_correction: None. This is a well-documented, standard feature on both platforms; once a title is downloaded at a chosen quality, no further chunk requests or ABR logic is invoked during playback.

article_title: How Your Phone's Fast Charging Works, and Why It Slows Down Near 80 Percent
claim: Standard lithium-ion cells have a maximum safe voltage of typically around 4.2 volts per cell.
source: Adafruit Learning System, "Voltages | Li-Ion & LiPoly Batteries"
required_correction: None. 4.2V (±50mV) per cell is the standard full-charge voltage for common lithium-ion (e.g., NMC/LCO) chemistries, as stated.

article_title: How Your Phone's Fast Charging Works, and Why It Slows Down Near 80 Percent
claim: Charging happens in two phases — constant current (CC), then constant voltage (CV) — with the CV transition typically starting somewhere around 70-80% charge.
source: Battery engineering references on CC/CV lithium-ion charging profiles
required_correction: None. CC/CV is the standard lithium-ion charging profile; the CV phase begins once cell voltage approaches the ~4.2V ceiling, which in practice commonly falls in the 70-80% state-of-charge range cited, though the exact transition point varies by cell design and charge rate.

article_title: How Your Phone's Fast Charging Works, and Why It Slows Down Near 80 Percent
claim: Pushing high current into a battery near its voltage ceiling risks lithium plating, where lithium deposits as metal on the anode instead of intercalating, permanently reducing capacity and creating a safety hazard in serious cases.
source: MDPI, "Predictive Framework for Lithium Plating Risk in Fast-Charging Lithium-Ion Batteries"
required_correction: None. Peer-reviewed literature confirms lithium plating occurs when anode overpotential drops below the lithium potential (more likely at high states of charge/high current), causing capacity fade, increased resistance, and — for irreversible/dendritic plating — safety risks including internal short circuits.

article_title: How Your Phone's Fast Charging Works, and Why It Slows Down Near 80 Percent
claim: USB Power Delivery is a widely supported fast-charging standard that negotiates a higher voltage/current between charger and phone, and can re-adjust dynamically based on battery temperature.
source: Tom's Hardware, "The USB Power Delivery (PD) Specification"
required_correction: None. USB-PD's negotiation protocol (source/sink capability exchange, PDO/RDO messages) and its continuous dynamic renegotiation based on device/thermal state are accurately described.

article_title: How Your Phone's Fast Charging Works, and Why It Slows Down Near 80 Percent
claim: Keeping a lithium-ion battery between roughly 20% and 80% for most of its life measurably extends usable lifespan compared to habitually running it from empty to completely full.
source: EEPower, "Why Lithium-Ion Batteries Last Longer at 20-80% SOC"
required_correction: None. Multiple industry summaries of battery-aging studies show meaningfully extended cycle life (often 2-3x or more) when charge is kept within a mid-range window versus full 0-100% cycling, consistent with the article's claim.

article_title: How Your Phone's Fast Charging Works, and Why It Slows Down Near 80 Percent
claim: Wireless charging is consistently slower than wired at a comparable wattage rating and generates noticeably more heat, due to energy lost in the induction coils on both sides.
source: Android Central, "Wireless charging vs. wired charging vs. 'Fast Charging': How do they compare in efficiency?"
required_correction: None, and if anything understated: wired charging is typically 85-95%+ efficient versus roughly 60-80% for wireless (Qi2 improves this to ~80-85%), meaning 20-30% of wireless charging energy is commonly lost as heat — a larger gap than the article's framing of "an extra layer of inefficiency" might suggest.

article_title: Inverter vs UPS for Home Power Backup — What Is the Real Difference
claim: A true online UPS keeps devices running continuously off its battery even during the moment power cuts, with effectively zero switchover time.
source: FSP Technology, "The importance of transfer time to UPS"
required_correction: None. Online (double-conversion) UPS topology continuously drives the load from its inverter off a DC bus that mains merely keeps charged, giving genuinely zero transfer time, exactly as described.

article_title: Inverter vs UPS for Home Power Backup — What Is the Real Difference
claim: Budget/line-interactive UPS units switch to battery within a few milliseconds of detecting a cut, fast enough that computers generally don't notice.
source: FSP Technology / Power Inspired, UPS transfer time explainers
required_correction: None. Line-interactive UPS transfer times are commonly documented in the 4-6 millisecond range, well within the sub-5ms threshold generally considered safe for computer power supplies, matching the article's claim.

article_title: Inverter vs UPS for Home Power Backup — What Is the Real Difference
claim: Home inverters have a switchover delay usually a fraction of a second to a couple of seconds.
required_correction: Plausible and consistent with general knowledge of household inverter changeover relays (electromechanical relay-based switching commonly runs a few hundred milliseconds to a couple of seconds; some electronic changeovers are faster), but no dedicated authoritative spec sheet or standards source was located in this pass to pin down an exact figure. Consider citing a specific manufacturer datasheet (e.g., Luminous, Microtek) for a precise number.

article_title: Inverter vs UPS for Home Power Backup — What Is the Real Difference
claim: Converting battery DC power to household AC through an inverter loses some energy as heat, typically in the range of 10-20% depending on the inverter's quality and age.
source: SolaxPower / Innotinum, inverter efficiency guides
required_correction: The lower end of the stated range overstates typical modern loss. Good-quality modern inverters commonly run 95-98% efficient (2-5% loss); the 10-20% loss figure applies more specifically to older, budget, or off-grid units (commonly cited around 85-90% efficient). Suggest narrowing to something like "2-15%, with older or budget units at the higher end" rather than implying 10-20% is typical across the board.

article_title: Inverter vs UPS for Home Power Backup — What Is the Real Difference
claim: Older flooded lead-acid inverter batteries need the water level checked periodically, and running them dry shortens battery life significantly.
source: Trojan Battery Company, "Flooded Lead Acid Batteries" quick watering guide
required_correction: None. Flooded lead-acid battery maintenance guides consistently confirm that plates exposed above the electrolyte level (from water loss during charging/gassing) cause accelerated degradation and require periodic distilled-water top-ups.

article_title: RO vs UV Water Purifier — Which One Your Water Actually Needs
claim: Water below roughly 300 ppm TDS is usually fine without RO, while water above 500 ppm is where RO becomes necessary rather than optional.
source: Bureau of Indian Standards, IS 10500:2012 Drinking Water Specification; WHO TDS palatability classification
required_correction: The 500 ppm figure matches BIS IS 10500's official "acceptable limit" for TDS (with a permissible limit of 2000 ppm in the absence of an alternative source) — so "above 500 ppm RO becomes necessary" is a reasonable practical reading of the standard. The 300 ppm figure, however, is an industry/WHO-palatability rule of thumb (WHO classifies <300 ppm as "excellent"), not an official Indian regulatory threshold; worth clarifying that 300 ppm is a general guideline rather than a BIS cutoff, as the article itself does note with "general reference" language.

article_title: RO vs UV Water Purifier — Which One Your Water Actually Needs
claim: UV purification disrupts the DNA of bacteria, viruses, and other microorganisms, and does nothing for dissolved salts or heavy metals — it doesn't remove or reduce TDS at all.
source: Wikipedia, "Ultraviolet germicidal irradiation" (mechanism sourced to water-treatment engineering literature)
required_correction: None. UV inactivates microbes by damaging nucleic acids (forming pyrimidine dimers) and is explicitly documented as not removing dissolved organics, inorganic compounds, or particles — meaning it does not reduce TDS, exactly as the article states.

article_title: RO vs UV Water Purifier — Which One Your Water Actually Needs
claim: RO membranes typically need replacement every 12-24 months depending on usage and input water quality, while UV lamps degrade and need replacement roughly once a year.
source: Arthur Heating & Air, RO filter maintenance guide; Fresh Water Systems, UV system maintenance guide
required_correction: The UV lamp figure (~12 months / ~9,000 hours rated life) matches sources closely. The RO membrane figure is on the shorter end of what's commonly cited — most maintenance guides put typical RO membrane life at 24-36 months (2-3 years), with 12-18 months reserved for budget membranes or poor input water and up to 48 months for premium membranes with good pre-filtration. Consider widening the stated range to roughly 12-36 months to better reflect the commonly cited spread.

article_title: RO vs UV Water Purifier — Which One Your Water Actually Needs
claim: RO wastes a significant amount of water in the filtration process — for every litre of purified water, a noticeable amount goes down the drain as reject water.
source: Waterfilterguru, "What to Know about Reverse Osmosis Waste Water"
required_correction: None. Traditional domestic RO systems are commonly documented as discarding roughly 3-4 liters (sometimes up to 9) of reject water per liter of purified water produced, confirming the article's "noticeable amount" characterization, though the article could optionally cite this specific ratio for concreteness.

article_title: RO vs UV Water Purifier — Which One Your Water Actually Needs
claim: RO forces water through a very fine membrane that physically blocks dissolved solids, and also removes bacteria and viruses as a side effect of the filtration, though that's not its core purpose.
source: General reverse osmosis membrane filtration engineering references (semi-permeable membrane rejection of dissolved ions/pathogens)
required_correction: None (source cited is illustrative of general membrane science rather than RO-specific; the mechanism described — semi-permeable membrane physically rejecting dissolved ions and, incidentally, larger biological particles like bacteria/viruses — is standard, uncontested water-treatment engineering).

article_title: How to Choose Between a Split AC and a Window AC for a Small Room
claim: Inverter technology adjusts compressor speed continuously instead of switching fully on and off, using less electricity over a cooling season than older non-inverter units of the same star rating.
source: Hitachi Cooling & Heating, "The Difference Between Fixed Speed vs Inverter"
required_correction: None. Industry sources document inverter (variable-speed) compressors reducing consumption meaningfully versus fixed-speed on/off cycling — figures cited range roughly 30-50% depending on comparison basis — supporting the article's general claim.

article_title: How to Choose Between a Split AC and a Window AC for a Small Room
claim: A 1-ton unit is usually sufficient for a small bedroom of roughly 100-120 sq ft, in either window or split form.
source: Haier India, "How to Calculate AC Tonnage for Your Room"
required_correction: None. Standard Indian sizing guides consistently place 1-ton AC as appropriate for roughly 100-120 sq ft rooms under typical conditions (no heavy direct sun, standard ceiling height, up to ~3 occupants), matching the article, which itself correctly flags heavier sun exposure or more occupants as reasons to size up.

article_title: How to Choose Between a Split AC and a Window AC for a Small Room
claim: A star rating (implying the BEE star-rating system) exists for both window and split ACs in India, with higher stars meaning less electricity use over its lifetime for the same tonnage.
source: Press Information Bureau, Government of India — BEE Star Labelling Programme results for split and window ACs
required_correction: None. BEE's mandatory star-labelling programme (under the Ministry of Power) applies to both split and window ACs sold in India, and PIB documents concrete efficiency improvements tied to higher star ratings, consistent with the article's claim.

article_title: How to Choose Between a Split AC and a Window AC for a Small Room
claim: A portable AC typically costs more to run for the same cooling output and is noisier than a split, since its compressor sits inside the room too.
required_correction: The "compressor is inside the room" part is definitionally true of portable AC design and reasonably implies more in-room noise than a split. The "costs more to run for the same cooling output" efficiency claim is plausible (single-hose portable units lose efficiency to negative-pressure infiltration of unconditioned air) but was not confirmed against a dedicated comparative source in this pass — recommend citing a specific SEER/EER comparison or manufacturer test data if precision matters here.

article_title: How to Reduce Your Electricity Bill Without Changing Your Lifestyle Much
claim: Setting the AC to 24-26°C instead of 18-20°C is often the single biggest AC-related saving available, since each degree lower makes the compressor work harder and longer.
source: Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) statements reported via Deccan Chronicle / Tribune India; power ministry proposals on AC default temperature
required_correction: None. BEE's director general has publicly pushed 24°C as the recommended default AC setting, and government/BEE figures cited in reporting put savings at roughly 6% per degree Celsius raised (and around 24% moving from 20°C to 24°C), directly supporting the article's claim.

article_title: How to Reduce Your Electricity Bill Without Changing Your Lifestyle Much
claim: Many Indian electricity boards bill in slabs, where the per-unit rate increases once monthly consumption crosses certain thresholds, so the last few units of a high-consumption month can cost more per unit than the first.
source: State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC) tariff structures, as summarized by ElectricBillTool
required_correction: None. Telescopic/progressive slab billing (each successive consumption band charged at a higher per-unit rate, set annually by each state's SERC) is the standard billing structure across Indian DISCOMs, confirming the article's claim exactly.

article_title: How to Reduce Your Electricity Bill Without Changing Your Lifestyle Much
claim: Rooftop solar with net metering has become more affordable in recent years with state subsidy schemes in many parts of India.
source: ClearTax, "PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana: Apply Online, Eligibility, Installation Subsidies, Benefits"
required_correction: None. The central PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana offers subsidies up to ₹78,000 for 3kW+ residential rooftop systems, uses net metering, and several states layer additional subsidies on top — matching the article's claim, though naming the scheme directly would strengthen the article.

article_title: How to Reduce Your Electricity Bill Without Changing Your Lifestyle Much
claim: A growing number of Indian electricity boards are piloting or rolling out time-of-day tariffs, where electricity costs more during peak evening hours and less during off-peak periods.
source: Press Information Bureau, Government of India — Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules on Time of Day Tariff
required_correction: None. Central rules mandate ToD tariffs (peak hours 10-20% above normal, solar/off-peak hours 10-20% below) for large commercial/industrial consumers from April 2024 and for most other consumers (excluding agricultural) from April 2025, with domestic-level rollout tied to the ongoing smart meter deployment — matching the article's "piloting or rolling out" framing.

article_title: How to Reduce Your Electricity Bill Without Changing Your Lifestyle Much
claim: A 5-star AC uses less electricity over its lifetime than a 3-star unit of the same tonnage, even though it costs more upfront.
source: Press Information Bureau, Government of India — BEE Star Labelling Programme efficiency improvement results
required_correction: None. BEE's own published results on the star labelling programme document a clear inverse relationship between star rating and energy consumption for both split and window ACs, directly supporting this claim.

article_title: How to Reduce Your Electricity Bill Without Changing Your Lifestyle Much
claim: Switching from old incandescent or CFL bulbs to LED uses a fraction of the electricity for the same brightness and lasts far longer, making up its higher upfront cost over time.
source: Wikipedia, "LED lamp" (efficacy and lifespan figures sourced to lighting industry/DOE data)
required_correction: None. LEDs (up to ~200+ lm/W) are roughly 12-20x more efficient than incandescent (10-17 lm/W) and meaningfully more efficient than CFL (50-100 lm/W); LED lifespan (~50,000 hours) is roughly 50x that of incandescent (~1,000 hours) and 3-4x that of CFL (~15,000 hours), fully supporting the article's claim.
